handoff_intake_phases_ms.description: @internal On a turn that the session's client handed over (turn_start_resume_kind is turn_handoff), how long its turn_handoff control request waited from its arrival on the session server's SSE stream (--sdk-url) until the input loop read it, in integer ms on the monotonic clock, split into parts that frame_intake_phases_ms explains: startup_wait, control_requests_ahead and user_frames_ahead, each absent when 0, and before_read (the rest), always present. The values sum to the wait. Present only on results that carry turn_start_resume_kind. Absent on a claude-code-server tenant, when the host had handled too much since the arrival to say what the request waited behind, and from older producers.

process_turn_index.description: @internal Number of earlier turns of this CLI process that sent a main-conversation model request: 0 is the process's first turn to reach the model, not the conversation's first. Turns that sent a request and then were stopped, deferred a tool or failed with an error subtype count but carry no value, so values can skip. Where one process hosts several sessions, each has its own count, from 0 each time the process starts hosting it. Present where time_to_request_phases_ms is. A worker that Anthropic hosts, with telemetry on, also sends it when a model turn ends in a result of this subtype with is_error true (an API error, a refused structured output). That result has none of the time_to_request_ or process_ fields beside it. If that turn sent no request, the value is the one its request would have had, so the next turn repeats it.

time_to_request_cpu_ms.description: @internal CPU time (user plus system) the CLI process used from turn start until it sent the turn's first main-conversation model request. Normally that is the time_to_request_ms window; if that request was abandoned for a new call (not an ordinary retry), time_to_request_ms runs on to the new one and this does not. Near time_to_request_ms, the window was mostly computing; near 0, mostly waiting. It adds up all threads, so it can exceed the window, and leaves out child processes, such as a command a tool runs. Unrelated work counts, such as the request that names the session (usually in its first turn). On a virtual machine, time the host spends restoring memory can count as CPU time, so a high value alone does not mean JavaScript work. Present where time_to_request_phases_ms is, unless the runtime reports no resource usage or the process hosts other sessions too.

time_to_request_loop_lag_ms.description: @internal The longest single stall of the session's thread between turn start and the turn's first main-conversation model request, measured as how late a 50 ms timer fired: the real stall can be up to 50 ms longer, so one under 50 ms can read 0, and a few ms is timer noise. JavaScript ran without a break, or the thread waited inside a blocking call (a synchronous file read or child process), or the whole process was paused; time_to_request_cpu_ms below this value means one of the last two, though on a virtual machine a pause while the host restores memory can look like CPU time. Any work on the thread counts: the request that names the session (usually in its first turn), or another session's where several share the thread. Only the first two minutes are measured. Present where time_to_request_phases_ms is.

time_to_request_major_faults.description: @internal Major page faults (waits for memory to be read from disk) by the process in the time_to_request_cpu_ms window; Windows also counts faults needing no disk read. On a virtual machine, memory the host restores is not counted: the machine never sees those faults. Present where time_to_request_cpu_ms is.

process_rss_mib_turn_start.description: @internal Resident memory of the CLI process at turn start, in whole MiB, as its kernel counts it (VmRSS in /proc/self/status). From the process's second turn on, it shows what stayed resident through the idle time since the turn before. Child processes, such as a command a tool runs or an MCP server, are left out. On a virtual machine it is the guest kernel's count, not what the host holds for the machine. Sent only by a worker that Anthropic hosts (never by a self-hosted runner, a BYOC environment, a session that Claude Desktop starts or a local run), and only with telemetry on. On such a worker it is present, always with process_rss_mib_result, where time_to_request_loop_lag_ms is, on Linux (not WSL), unless /proc/self/status cannot be read or lacks VmRSS, or the process hosts other sessions too.

process_anon_mib_turn_start.description: @internal The anonymous part of process_rss_mib_turn_start (RssAnon): memory with no file behind it, such as heaps, stacks and code the JavaScript engine compiles while running. Mapped files, such as the executable, are left out. Present where process_rss_mib_turn_start is, if the kernel gives it.

process_rss_mib_result.description: @internal As process_rss_mib_turn_start, read again after the turn, just before this result is built: the level the turn leaves behind.

process_anon_mib_result.description: @internal The anonymous part of process_rss_mib_result; see process_anon_mib_turn_start. Present where process_rss_mib_result is, if the kernel gives it.

process_peak_rss_mib.description: @internal The most memory the process has had resident from its start until this result (VmHWM), in whole MiB. It is not the peak of this turn alone: a later turn repeats an earlier peak unless it went higher. Present where process_rss_mib_result is, if the kernel gives it.

process_cpu_ms_between_turns.description: @internal CPU time (user plus system, all threads, without child processes) the CLI process used from the end of its previous turn to this turn's start: mostly what it costs while no turn runs. A turn ends after its last frame and its turn-end hooks. Work it left running in the background counts here, as do this turn's steps ahead of turn start, such as re-reading the tool list. To get CPU time per second, add these up over many results and divide by the sum of their process_wall_ms_between_turns, which always comes with it. Present where process_cpu_ms_turn is, from the process's second turn of any kind on (process_turn_index can still be 0), unless the previous turn was abandoned midway and so never ended.

process_wall_ms_between_turns.description: @internal The time that passed in the process_cpu_ms_between_turns stretch, by a clock that never runs backward. Time while the process is stopped counts; time while its virtual machine is paused may not.

process_cpu_ms_turn.description: @internal CPU time, counted as in process_cpu_ms_between_turns, from this turn's start until just before this result is built, so what the turn does after that is in neither stretch. The stretch includes the waits for the model and for tools. It always comes with process_wall_ms_turn. Sent only by the workers named under process_rss_mib_turn_start. On them it is present where time_to_request_loop_lag_ms is, unless the runtime reports no resource usage or the process hosts other sessions too.

process_wall_ms_turn.description: @internal The time that passed in the process_cpu_ms_turn stretch, by the same clock as process_wall_ms_between_turns.

process_cpu_ms_streaming.description: @internal CPU time, counted as in process_cpu_ms_between_turns, that the process used inside process_wall_ms_streaming. It is part of process_cpu_ms_turn. It holds what handling the streamed replies cost while they streamed, but not what the CLI does with a reply once its stream has ended. It also holds whatever else the process did meanwhile, such as a tool that starts before the reply ends, a subagent, a side request, telemetry or garbage collection. It always comes with process_wall_ms_streaming, main_stream_count and main_stream_event_count; main_stream_chunk_count can be missing. Sent only by the workers named under process_rss_mib_turn_start. On them it is present where process_cpu_ms_turn is, if a stream opened on the turn and each of its windows could be measured.

process_wall_ms_streaming.description: @internal How long, within the process_cpu_ms_turn stretch and by its clock, a response stream of a main-conversation model request was open: from the stream's first event until the CLI stopped reading it, whether it ended, failed or was aborted. The wait for the first event is not in it. Summed over the turn's requests; time in which two such streams were open counts once. The stream of a subagent, of a side request or of a compaction opens nothing.

main_stream_count.description: @internal How many streams process_wall_ms_streaming covers: one for each attempt of a main-conversation model request that brought a first event, so a retry after that counts again.

main_stream_event_count.description: @internal How many stream events the API sent on those streams, as tengu_api_success's streamEventCount counts them: keepalive pings that the CLI makes up itself are left out. A stream still open when this result is built adds none.

main_stream_chunk_count.description: @internal In how many chunks the runtime's fetch handed over the bodies of those streams. It is not the number of socket reads, several of which can make one chunk. Against main_stream_event_count it shows how the API's events arrive grouped, though the two do not divide evenly: a chunk can end inside an event, keepalive comments and pings are chunks that bring no event, and a stream that failed or was aborted can count one chunk whose events were never read. Absent, never 0, when a stream's chunks were not counted, as on Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry and Mantle, with the byte watchdog off, or for a stream still open when this result is built.

input_attachments_detail.description: @internal What the input_attachments phase of time_to_request_phases_ms did on the turn, to tell a wait inside one attachment producer from a process that was busy. The producers are the calls of maybe() in getAttachments; their labels are a closed list, and a producer's time includes the computing of the others that run beside it. slowest_producer is the label of the one that took longest from its start to its result, among those that began within the phase, and slowest_producer_ms is that time; a background agent's pass that begins within the phase is timed with the turn's own (a new process's first turn has none), and its re-reads are not counted. Where slowest_producer_ms is well above cpu_ms that producer most likely waited (on a file, the network or a child process); a time_to_request_loop_lag_ms near slowest_producer_ms says instead that the thread itself stood still about that long (a blocking call, or a paused process). Where it is not well above cpu_ms the label tells little. cpu_ms and major_faults are time_to_request_cpu_ms's and time_to_request_major_faults's counters over this phase alone and are read the same way: cpu_ms far below the phase's time means the process was not computing; at or above it means computing, without saying whose. Where cpu_ms is absent, the phase's own time is what there is to compare slowest_producer_ms with. changed_files_reread is how many files the changed_files producer set out to read again in full because their modification time was later than the one recorded when the conversation last wrote or edited them (0 when it read none again, whether or not any file was a candidate; absent when the conversation's record of files was empty or the producer did not run). Present on turns where the input_attachments phase started, unless nothing of it is known. cpu_ms and major_faults are absent wherever time_to_request_cpu_ms is absent, and when the turn's first model request went out before the phase ended. touch_compare counts how the changed_files producer's compares ended in the main thread's pass (a subagent's are not counted). A compare checks a touched file against what the conversation last saw (its size, then its bytes), before deciding whether to read it again. same: the text had not changed, so it was not read again. differs: it had, so it was read again. partial_view and already_compared: the file was not compared (the conversation has seen only part of it or an older copy, or it was compared once already since the conversation last read or wrote it) and was read again. The rest are why a compare declined and the file was read again: link_on_path (the file could not be shown to be the one its path names: on Linux a symbolic link on the way, or a landing through the outputs link that the read check did not judge; or the file swapped or removed meanwhile), leaf_link (the open met a symbolic link: at the file, or on macOS anywhere on the way), nlink (the file has a second hard link), not_regular, oversize, enoent (the file was gone) and other (anything else, errors included). via_outputs_link counts those of same and differs that were reached through the hosted container's outputs link, from /mnt/user-data/outputs to /mnt/attach/outputs. Whole numbers; a zero count is left out, and touch_compare is absent when nothing was counted.

resume_store_confirm_detail.description: @internal How the resume_store_confirm phase of time_to_request_phases_ms was spent. Present where that phase is, in a session whose transcript goes to a hosted store: on the result of a handed-off turn whose lines were confirmed and that went on to a model request. A wait that ends its turn (the lines not stored, or the turn stopped meanwhile) is therefore not in the measure. The four _ms values sum to that phase exactly. write_ms: the transcript write, until the carried lines are in the queue of the lane that uploads transcript rows (POST /worker/internal-events, one POST out at a time); a POST that is out during the write is counted in posts and rows, but that part of its time is in write_ms only. The other three split the wait for that lane to empty. ahead_ms: a POST was out that held only rows queued before the hand-off's write began, one already out at that moment included. post_ms: any other POST was out, timed by the client from before the body is encoded to the response, each retry included. other_ms: no POST was out (a backoff between retries, picking and sizing the next batch, a busy event loop), plus rounding, any POST still out when the wait was cut short, and the time of POSTs after the 64th. posts: POST attempts that ended between the start of the write and the end of the wait; failed_posts: those that did not go through. rows_ahead: rows the lane had accepted and the store had not yet confirmed when the write began, queued or in a POST already out; rows written earlier but kept back for a compaction's summary count from when they are queued. rows: rows queued since then that a POST delivered, the carried lines among them.

first_request_input_tokens.description: @internal Input tokens of the model call whose send time is request_sent_wall_ms: input_tokens + cache_read_input_tokens + cache_creation_input_tokens from that call's message_start. Lets a consumer group turn latency by prompt size. Present only with request_sent_wall_ms, and only when the sum is above zero; absent from older producers.

user_message_server_received_wall_ms.description: @internal The server_received_wall_ms of the user message that user_message_uuid names, copied unchanged, so the session server can measure from its own receipt to request_sent_wall_ms (two machines' clocks) without keeping the receipt time. Present only with request_sent_wall_ms, and only when that message carried a positive finite number there; absent from older producers.

frame_received_wall_ms.description: @internal Date.now() (epoch ms) when the triggering send's frame arrived on a session reading its input from the session server's SSE stream (--sdk-url), before the input loop read it. With frame_enqueued_wall_ms and turn_started_wall_ms it splits the stretch between the server's persist and request_sent_wall_ms into transit, the input loop's handling of the frame, its wait on the command queue, and the turn's own work. Present only together with request_sent_wall_ms, and only when the transport recorded the receipt; absent on a local stdin host and from older producers.

frame_enqueued_wall_ms.description: @internal Date.now() (epoch ms) when the input loop put the triggering send's frame on the command queue. Present exactly when frame_received_wall_ms is.

turn_started_wall_ms.description: @internal Date.now() (epoch ms) when the turn's clock started: the anchor duration_ms, ttft_ms, ttft_stream_ms, time_to_request_ms, first_content_frame_ms, first_stream_post_ms and first_stream_post_ack_ms are measured from. Present exactly when frame_received_wall_ms is.

frame_intake_phases_ms.description: @internal How the triggering send's frame spent the time from frame_received_wall_ms to frame_enqueued_wall_ms, in integer ms per step: before_read (until the input loop read the frame; a frame received more than once counts from the earliest receipt no earlier copy already took), and, carved out of before_read where the loop could tell them apart, startup_wait (the part before the input loop existed, the worker still starting), control_requests_ahead (the part the loop spent handling control requests before it read the frame) and user_frames_ahead (the part it spent on earlier user frames, each from its read until the loop moved on, at its delivery or its parking), so that before_read keeps only the rest (frames handled without being noted, and everything when no split could be made); then dedup, flag_settle, receive_hook, attachments, admission_wait (held behind a pending model switch, a pending MCP server-set change, start-up work the worker still owed its first turn, or an earlier held frame), admit_check (the host's decision whether to queue the frame, when it had to be awaited), and other (the rest). Steps that did not run are absent; before_read and other are always present. The values sum to frame_enqueued_wall_ms minus frame_received_wall_ms, unless other or before_read came out negative and was set to 0. Present exactly when frame_received_wall_ms is, except from older producers.

turn_start_phases_ms.description: @internal How the time from frame_enqueued_wall_ms to turn_started_wall_ms was spent, in integer ms per step of the host's work through its message queue. Each step is where the host was at the time, which for part of the stretch may be an earlier message's turn. The steps: idle (the host was not working through its queue), earlier_turn (an earlier turn still running, including its work after its result), after_turn (the host's work after an earlier turn ended and before it took the next message: recording the outcome, writing the transcript and acknowledgements, and releasing the queue; also its handling of a crash), background_wait (waiting on background tasks before looking at the queue again), entry_joins (other waits when the host starts on its queue, before it may take a message), sdk_mcp_update (the claude -p host updating its SDK MCP servers when it starts on its queue), loop_top (reloading plugins that changed, at the start of each pass over the queue), session_start_wait (waiting for the plugins' first session.start hook, and taking the message off the queue), first_command (the claude -p host's waits for its plugin registry and a Projects mount before the first message it takes each time it starts on its queue), mcp_prewait (waiting for MCP servers still connecting, before that same first message), repo_wait (a claude-code-server session waiting for its repository before a turn), turn_joins (before every turn: waiting for a Projects mount and for SDK or newly added MCP servers), tool_pool (building the turn's tools), commit (marking the message taken and setting up its turn), after_arm (waiting for a cleared permission prompt's record to be written, and the host's other work once the turn is set up), turn_gate (work the host requires before every turn), turn_open (the host's turn-start hook and other turn setup), engine_setup (getting the engine for the turn; on the claude -p host's first turn, building its session), tool_reread (re-reading tools, MCP clients and settings for the turn), cwd (switching to the turn's working directory), and other (the rest: rounding, and the wall clock running ahead of the monotonic one). Values are rounded so that they add up: each is within 1 ms of its step's time, a step that comes out as 0 is absent, and other is always present. The values sum to turn_started_wall_ms minus frame_enqueued_wall_ms, except that they can exceed it, usually by 1 ms from rounding and by more if the wall clock stepped back. Present only when frame_received_wall_ms is, and absent from older producers.

turn_start_control_requests_ms.description: @internal Of the time from frame_enqueued_wall_ms to turn_started_wall_ms, the integer ms in which the claude -p host's message reader was held by control requests (such as mcp_set_servers or set_permission_mode) instead of reading the next message; for a request handled in the background, only its start counts. The host can keep working toward the turn meanwhile, so this overlaps turn_start_phases_ms and is not part of its sum. Absent when 0. A claude-code-server tenant does not time control requests, so its results never have this field.

flag_fetch_kick.description: @internal One of FLAG_FETCH_KICKS, a string here so that list can change: whether this process started its start-up feature-flag fetch before the wait for it, or why not: the same value as system:init's startup_timing.flag_fetch_kick. started_in_init_* and started_after_init_*: it did, inside init() or right after. not_asked_warm: the flag cache was warm and nothing asked for an early start. settings_pending_*: settings that could change the fetch were still to be applied. launch_excluded: not a launch that starts it early. not_eligible: interactive, or no wait is budgeted. An _empty or _warm ending is the flag cache at that moment. Present only where time_to_request_from_spawn_ms is, and only when start-up judged it.

process_start_tuning.description: @internal Which runtime tuning variables the CLI process was started with, one bit for each that was set and not empty: 1 BUN_GC_TIMER_INTERVAL, 2 MIMALLOC_PURGE_HOLES_MIN_INTERVAL, 4 BUN_IDLE_GC_SECONDS, 8 MIMALLOC_PURGE_DELAY, 16 BUN_JSC_useFTLJIT, 32 BUN_JSC_percentCPUPerMBForEdenTimer, 64 BUN_JSC_percentCPUPerMBForFullTimer. It says that a name was set, never to what. It is taken once, as the process starts, because that is when the runtime reads them: a worker adopted from a warm spare reports the spare's own variables, not the ones its claim brought. Sent only by the workers named under process_rss_mib_turn_start, unless the process hosts other sessions too. They put it on a session's results as they write them, whatever the subtype and whether or not the turn sent a request. A result that reports a failed start or a fatal error is written raw and has none.

process_start_purge_delay_ms.description: @internal MIMALLOC_PURGE_DELAY, in milliseconds, as the CLI process was started with it. Taken with process_start_tuning and sent only beside it. Absent where the variable was unset or empty, and where its text is anything but one to seven digits, so no text can travel: bit 8 of process_start_tuning still says that it was set.

process_garbage_collections.description: @internal Garbage collections on the CLI process's main thread, counted from early start-up, before its main modules load. to_first_message: up to the start of the process's first turn, whether a message or start-up itself (a resumed turn, say) began it; absent if no turn began first or its count failed. to_first_result: up to this result, including to_first_message's. A worker claimed from a warm spare counts from the spare's own start, so both include its wait for the claim. Each gives eden (collections of young objects only; under Bun the process's first also marks the whole heap), full (collections of the whole heap), wall_ms (their summed wall-clock time, not CPU time) and heap_after_mib (heap in use after the last one; absent if none ran). A collection still running at either moment is not in that count. Only on the process's first numbered result (result_index 0) within an hour of its start, only when the process, or the warm spare it was claimed from, started with CLAUDE_CODE_COUNT_GARBAGE_COLLECTIONS=1, and only from cloud workers that Anthropic hosts, with telemetry on, never from a process that hosts other sessions.

api_error_code.description: @internal The api_error_code of the API error that ended the turn (see SDKAssistantMessage.api_error_code): the server's error.details.error_code when it is an identifier. Absent when the turn did not end on an API error or the response carried no code.

api_error_origin.description: @internal The api_error_origin of the API error that ended the turn (see SDKAssistantMessage.api_error_origin): first_party when Anthropic's own API sent the response. Absent when the turn did not end on an API error or the origin is anything else; treat an unknown value as absent.

api_error.description: @internal The api_error of the API error that ended the turn (see SDKAssistantMessage.api_error). Absent when the turn did not end on an API error or the error has no typed kind; treat an unknown value as absent.

total_cost_usd.description: Cumulative estimated cost in USD for this query() call, covering the same query-pipeline calls as modelUsage and sharing its lifecycle: cumulative across turns in streaming-input sessions — each result carries the running total so far, so read the latest result rather than summing across results. Crash/startup-error results may carry zeroed values, a resumed or forked session continues from the total its transcript saved, when it has one (so the first result already carries the earlier turns; maxBudgetUsd counts only the spend since this query() call started or last /clear), and a mid-session /clear resets the running total. An estimate, not a billing statement.

usage.description: MAIN AGENT LOOP ONLY — excludes Task subagent, sidechain, and auxiliary model calls, and is per-turn in streaming-input sessions. Prefer modelUsage for token/cost accounting.

modelUsage.description: Per-model totals for every model call made through the query pipeline during this query() call — main loop, Task subagents, sidechains, and internal calls such as compaction and Workflow agents. Cumulative across turns in streaming-input sessions: each result carries the running total so far, so read the latest result rather than summing across results. Internal helper calls outside the query pipeline (e.g. the permission classifier, token-count probes) are excluded; crash/startup-error results may carry zeroed usage, a resumed or forked session continues from the totals its transcript saved, when it has them (so the first result already carries the earlier turns), and a mid-session /clear resets the running total. The correct field for token/cost accounting; treat it as an estimate, not a billing statement.

model_usage_since_last_result.description: @internal Per-model usage and cost of the calls this process counted since it wrote its previous result (since it started, for its first), keyed and shaped like modelUsage and covering the same calls. Sum it over a conversation's results instead of subtracting modelUsage totals: within a conversation each call is stated on at most one result, whatever a resume or a kill does to modelUsage. Calls that finish after a result (a background subagent, a late title call) are stated on the next result, and a /clear's own result states what was counted before it. Nothing is carried from one process to the next, so what a process counted after its last result is stated nowhere. That includes the finished calls of a turn in flight when the process is shut down or killed, even where another process carries the turn on and writes its result. A result whose write fails loses its usage too (result_index shows the gap). A Workflow agent that runs as a cloud session of its own is counted here, as in modelUsage, and that session's own results state it too. costBasis, canonicalModel and provider are the latest request's. A model with nothing counted is left out; {} means nothing was counted. Set by a stream-json or --sdk-url run on the results it numbers as it writes them; a result relayed from another process keeps what that process set. Not set on error results numbered by hand (a start-up failure, an error that escapes the run), by --output-format json and text runs, or by older versions. Absent is not {}.

subagent_stats.description: @internal Running totals of the subagents the Agent tool started this session; see SDKSubagentStats.

safety_stops.description: @internal How many times a safety system has stopped one of this session's model calls made through the query pipeline (main loop, subagents, forked skills, compaction and other internal calls), as a running total since the session started in this process; two sessions in one process keep separate counts. Counted: a response that ends on stop_reason refusal, whether Claude Code then shows it, retries it or re-sends it to another model; a refusal that the API itself answered on a fallback model; output that the API's content filter stopped for good (the stop ends the call); and, where the build can recognise it (public builds cannot), a server-side safety monitor's block (api_error safety_monitor_blocked). It counts these events, not calls: one call can add a refusal answered on a fallback model and then that model's own refusal. 0 means that none of these was seen; a kind of stop that this version does not know is not counted. Never sum across results. It is never saved, so a resumed session starts at 0 again, and a mid-session /clear zeroes it: over a stored log that spans a restart, a resume or a /clear, any result above 0 means a stop happened, and a later 0 does not cancel it. Present, 0 included, on every result that carries a turn's measured totals. Absent on the zeroed results that stand in for a crashed, cut or never-started turn, on Remote Control's results and from older producers, where it says nothing: absent is not 0. A call still running when a result is written (a background subagent's) shows on the next result; a result held back while background subagents finished carries the count as of when it is written to the stream, never less than it was built with. Not counted inside the pipeline: a stop of the API's content filter that Claude Code answers by streaming the request again (so 0 does not rule one out), an organization's data-loss-prevention denial (api_error dlp_request_denied), a block by a cloud provider's own guardrail, an advisor's refusal inside a reply that ends normally. Not counted at all: model calls outside the query pipeline (e.g. the permission classifier, token-count probes) and work in other processes.

queued_turn_count.description: User-initiated sends still waiting in the command queue when this result was produced. Greater than 0 means at least one more user turn (and result) follows without further input, barring cancellation; 0 means none is pending, or the session is ending (end_session or a shutdown latched mid-turn discards the backlog). Queued sends may coalesce into fewer turns, so this counts pending sends, not remaining results. System-generated queue entries are not counted. Absent on fatal startup results and on surfaces without a command queue.

terminal_reason.description: Why the query loop terminated. Unset when the loop was bypassed (local slash command).

interrupted_by_shutdown.description: @internal The host of a multi-tenant worker shut the worker down while this turn ran. The shutdown was the first thing to abort the turn, and the turn is left for the session's next worker. The other frames of the ending, and terminal_reason, are the same as for a Stop from a client. Read this member to tell the two apart. A success result can have it, when the shutdown falls in a Stop hook. A result without it can also be the result of a shutdown. A shutdown that makes the turn write no interrupt marker does not set it, and older producers never set it.

result_index.description: Delivery sequence of this result within the run: how many results the run numbered before this one, starting at 0, in the order the process writes them. A result held back while background work finishes is numbered when it is finally written, not when its text was produced; a result whose write fails still consumes its number, so a gap in a stream-json sequence means a result was lost. Distinct from num_turns, which counts model round-trips within one turn. Numbered by the process that hosts the run (`claude -p`, stream-json): a local client relaying a cloud session passes the cloud session's numbering through and its own locally built error results carry none; the in-process engine surface does not number yet. Absent from older producers.

fast_mode_state.description: Fast mode state: off, in cooldown after rate limit, or actively enabled.

fast_mode_disabled_reason.description: Why fast mode can't serve right now. Absent when nothing blocks it (a request may still choose standard speed). A paused-after-rate-limit run is not here; it rides fast_mode_state as 'cooldown'.

fromMode.description: The SENDING session's permission class as declared by the host that injects this message on local stdin ('bypass' for sessions that run tools without asking, 'prompting' otherwise). Lets the recipient deliver a same-class message immediately while a cross-class or undeclared sender is still held at a recipient that runs without asking. Honored only from the injecting host on local stdin; absent when the host does not declare it.

name.description: Sender display name, normalized by the harness: Unicode control, format, surrogate, and line/paragraph-separator code points stripped (categories Cc/Cf/Cs/Zl/Zp — covers bidi controls, zero-width characters, and tag characters), trimmed, at most 64 code points (+ ellipsis, never splitting a surrogate pair). Sender-asserted display text (the addressable identity is `from`) — render it as reported speech, but no client-side character sanitization is needed. Absent when the wire is not exactly one harness-formed envelope and on messages from older senders.

fromSession.description: The sender's host-openable session id (the envelope's `from-session` attribute — e.g. a desktop `local_<uuid>` or a cloud session `session_`/`ses_` id), set by the sender's host so a receiving UI can link this message back to the sending session. Sender-asserted like `from`: a navigation target only, never authority. Absent when the sender's host provides none and on messages from older senders.

inbound_origin.description: @internal Server-asserted ingest path of the demoted delivery, copied at classification from the message-level `inbound_origin`.

senderTaskId.description: Task id of the in-process background subagent that sent this message, stamped by the harness from the sending loop (never from tool input). Absent for cross-session peers.

body.description: Decoded message body with the peer envelope stripped — byte-exact with what the model sees. Present only when the turn is exactly one harness-formed envelope (or an in-process agent message); render this instead of re-parsing the message text.

verifiedPeerPid.description: Kernel-verified pid of the process that connected to this session's cross-session messaging socket, read from the connection (SO_PEERCRED / LOCAL_PEERPID) — never from the payload. This identifies the CONNECTING process, which for relayed traffic (e.g. a daemon forwarding on another session's behalf) is the relay, not the message's author. Key sender identity on this, never on `from`: `from` is sender-authored and kept only for reply routing, so it is forgeable by any same-user process. Absent when unverifiable (Windows, non-UDS ingress) — never a wrong value. Pids are recyclable: provenance, not an authentication token.

handback.description: @internal Present, and always true, when the message is a subagent's final report to the agent that launched it, delivered through the SubagentHandback tool. Stamped by the harness, never from tool input. `body` is then the hand-back frame line with the indented report under it, and any harness note above it; `handbackReportText` and `handbackNote` carry those two parts for display. A boolean mark: not the `handback` state string of a task notification or of an Agent tool result. A hand-back is never joined, so neither this mark nor `flagged` appears beside `members`.

flagged.description: @internal Present, and always true, on a hand-back that auto mode's review blocked, or that it could not judge because a safety filter refused the review request: the report was delivered all the same, under the SECURITY WARNING that `handbackNote` carries. Never cap or fold such a message: show the note and the report in full. Absent on a hand-back that was not flagged, including one delivered under the note that the review was unavailable.

handbackNote.description: @internal On a hand-back: the note the harness composed above the frame line in `body`, without the indent. On a blocked report it quotes the review's reason, which can quote the report, so show it as untrusted text. Absent when there is no note.

handbackReportText.description: @internal On a hand-back: the subagent's report as the model reads it, under the frame line in `body`, without the indent. Draw it as a separate element from `handbackNote`: the two fields are their only boundary. Absent wherever `body` is and on a message that is not a hand-back.

members.description: @internal On a prompt that joins several queued messages from this sender: the joined messages in the order the model reads them, each with its own `body`. The origin's `body` is then absent. Absent on a message that was not joined and when any joined message had no `body`.

subkind.description: Present when the delivery is the fired stored prompt of a scheduled task/routine ('scheduled-trigger', stamped from server-asserted provenance, or declared by a local host for its own scheduled runs; the schedule attests storage, not authorship) or a coordinator co-member SendMessage delivery ('peer-send-message': model-authored text from another of the same user's sessions, verified by the server-stamped receiver co-membership — task-notification for prompt authority, but distinguishable so the receive-side crossSessionInbound setting can apply to it). The harness frames a scheduled-trigger delivery as the session's assigned task instead of the generic background-notification frame. Absent on webhook, PR-steward, plugin, and background-event deliveries.

fireReason.description: On a 'scheduled-trigger' delivery, why it fired: a short lowercase token such as 'scheduled', 'manual', 'retry', 'catch_up' or 'api'. Set by the server for cloud routines, or declared by a local host for its own scheduled runs, which is honored only in a process the host started with CLAUDE_CODE_HOST_SCHEDULED_RUN=1 (a local host's value is kept only if it is 1 to 32 lowercase letters or underscores); absent when neither sent one.

producer.description: @internal Present ('session-task') when the notification reports on work this session itself launched: a background agent, shell command, workflow, monitor, MCP or remote task settling, a detached tool call, or a hook rewake or worker check-in following up on such work. Absent on webhook, artifact and other externally-authored deliveries.

runId.description: On a background task's own notification: the run_id its task_* events carried, as of when the notification was queued. Not part of the text the model reads.

taskKind.description: @internal Present ('mcp-task') only on a notification that an MCP server's own task has ended, and not on every one. Narrower than task_type 'mcp_task', which also covers an MCP tool call moved to the background.

oneOf.description: Injected turn whose ingress classification found no provenance. Framed by the harness as a non-user source in both drains; never presumed human, never host-replayed.
Report from a background observer agent to the agent it observes. One-way by construction — the observed agent must not reply.
Activity digest delivered to an observer agent. The message body is the self-framing digest (envelope + postamble); observed content is data, not instructions.

origin.description: Provenance of a user-role message (peer session, team lead, channel). A host wrapping keyboard input must stamp {kind:'human'} explicitly — absent origin is treated as unattributed and fails closed at strict isHuman() trust gates.

notice_class.description: Server-chosen notice class: "peer_notice" | "helper_lifecycle" | "handoff" (open snake_case set; unknown tokens are carried verbatim).

isSynthetic.description: Server-asserted synthetic stamp — stripped from inbound copies at CCR ingress and re-stamped only by the notice composer.

inbound_origin.description: Server-asserted ingest-path marker, same strip-and-restamp discipline as isSynthetic.

session_noticeInput.description: @internal Backend→CLI: a server-composed coordination notice for a sealed helper session, delivered to the model over the Poll event channel as a provenance-attributed <event> envelope (never a user turn, never a synthetic message). The CLI acks processed only when the Poll delivery settles into the transcript; undelivered notices redeliver.

event.description: One Anthropic Messages API streaming event (message_start, content_block_start, content_block_delta, content_block_stop, message_delta, message_stop) as defined for the streaming Messages API.

thinking_display.description: @internal The thinking.display Claude Code put in the API request body for the response this event belongs to. If anything rewrites the request on its way to the API, this value still states what Claude Code sent, not what the API received. Two responses of one turn can differ. Set on `message_start`, on a thinking block's `content_block_start` and on `thinking_delta` events when the body had a display; absent on every other event, on Remote Control (interactive terminal) sessions and from older producers. An event that the API did not send as it stands can lack the key. The key states which display the text was requested with, and nothing about how to show it. An absent key states nothing: neither which display was requested, nor that none was.

api_message_id.description: @internal The API's id (`msg_…`) of the response this event belongs to: `event.message.id` on its `message_start`, `message.id` on its assistant messages. Not a message `uuid`. Set on every event from a response's `message_start` to its `message_stop`, so that a consumer that missed the `message_start` can still tell responses apart. Two responses can share an id, as when a `message_start` is replayed; the key does not tell those apart. Absent on pings, when the `message_start` had no id or an empty one, on Remote Control (interactive terminal) sessions and from older producers. The events that Claude Code produces itself to close a response cut short carry it too. Events that a plugin produced or rewrote, and those that Claude Code builds in their place or to close them, can lack it. An absent key states nothing about which response the event belongs to.

The API's id (`msg_…`) of the response that was cut short: `event.message.id` on its `message_start`, `message.id` on its assistant messages. Not a message `uuid`. Should two responses share an id, the one meant is the one this `message_stop` closes.

from_block_index.description: Blocks of the response at this index and above have no assistant message and never will. It is an `event.index` as on the response's `content_block_*` events, not a count of assistant messages. 0 means the whole response. Can be higher than every index the consumer has seen, and then there is nothing to remove.

abandoned_blocks.description: @internal Set on a `message_stop` that Claude Code produced itself, after it stopped reading the response that `message_stop` closes because the API's stream failed, stalled or ended early, or because the turn was interrupted. That response's content blocks at index `from_block_index` and above have no assistant message and will never get one, so a consumer that drew or stored them from stream events, and holds no assistant message for them, can remove them, even a block that has had its `content_block_stop`. Nothing is stated about lower blocks: some may have no assistant message, and what follows may repeat or replace them. What follows can be, among others, a retry (a new `message_start`), the same request without streaming (assistant messages under another id, with no `message_start` before them), an assistant message that reports the error, or nothing. A plugin can add content blocks of its own to a response, and those do get assistant messages under the same id, emitted before this event. Absent on every other `message_stop` (the API's own, one produced for a response that had arrived whole, one where Claude Code cannot be sure), on Remote Control (interactive terminal) sessions and from older producers. An absent key states nothing: a block with no assistant message yet may still get one.

text_runs_joined.description: @internal Set on the `message_start` of a response when CLAUDE_CODE_WEBSEARCH_CITATIONS is on in a non-interactive session. Each run of adjacent text blocks of that response gets one assistant message with one text block, which holds the joined text. Each entry of its `citations`, except a `web_search_result_location`, has `span_start` and `span_end`: the place of the cited block in the joined text, in Unicode code points, end exclusive. The `content_block_*` events still show each block of the run by its own index. A response that came without streaming has no `message_start`, and it is joined too.

user_message_uuid.description: Client uuid of the user message this turn is answering (submitMessage options.uuid), stamped on a non-ping stream event each time that send changes: the turn's FIRST non-ping stream event (normally the frame that triggers the turn's initial ack), and, for a turn started by a synthetic (meta) prompt, the first non-ping stream event after each queued user message folded in mid-turn takes the echo over (see SDKAssistantMessage.user_message_uuid for the rule) — so a consumer can bind the reply stream to the send it answers without waiting for the result. A turn started by a typed prompt stamps only its first non-ping stream event; independently, its first complete assistant message is stamped as well (see SDKAssistantMessage.user_message_uuid), so the same uuid may appear on both. Absent on every other stream event of the turn, on turns that neither had a client uuid nor folded a user message in, and from older producers.

user_message_uuids.description: Client uuids of every user message whose prompt this turn has consumed so far, in consumption order — all members of a prompt batch the host merged into this one turn (several messages sent close together run as one turn whose user_message_uuid is the LAST member's), then any user message folded into the turn before this frame — so a consumer that sent any of them can bind this reply to its own send by finding its uuid anywhere in the list. Always contains user_message_uuid; at most 64 entries. Present exactly when user_message_uuid is, on the same frames; absent from older producers (fall back to user_message_uuid).

resume_reason.description: Why this frame's turn continues one that a worker restart interrupted. Such a turn is the automatic re-run of the interrupted turn (CLAUDE_CODE_RESUME_INTERRUPTED_TURN), or one that goes on from the answer to the permission prompt the new worker took over, or from that turn's tool calls still in flight. The value is the host's CLAUDE_CODE_RESUME_REASON when it set one (host_draining, checkpoint_restore, container_recreated, …), else 'interrupted_turn'. Stamped on the same reply frames as user_message_uuid (which on such a turn names the interrupted turn's own last user prompt), so a consumer can tell its first reply from the interrupted attempt's. Absent on every other turn (also one that goes on from the answer to any other permission prompt), on thinking_tokens frames, and from older producers.

stream_eventOutput.description: An incremental streaming event for the assistant message being generated, emitted only when partial messages are requested (--include-partial-messages). The complete assistant message still follows as its own message.

no_response.description: Present only when the API sent no response headers within the first-byte window (CLAUDE_STREAM_FIRST_BYTE_TIMEOUT_MS): waited_ms is how long the failed attempt waited for headers, retry_wait_ms how long the retry will wait for them. For this cause max_retries is its own cap (normally one retry), not the session budget.

system_api_retryOutput.description: Emitted when an API request fails with a retryable error and will be retried after a delay. error_status is null for connection errors (e.g. timeouts) that had no HTTP response.

run_id.description: Id of one run of the task: equal on every task_* event, background_tasks_changed entry and saved notification (its origin.runId) of that run. A resumed task keeps its task_id and gets a new one. The run ids of one task sort, by plain string comparison, in the order the runs opened; a frame that names a run sorting before the one a reader shows is late. Nothing else about the format is promised. Absent for a task this process did not register, and from CLIs that predate it.

subagent_type.description: Agent type of a local_agent task, such as "general-purpose" or a custom agent's name; "main-session" for a backgrounded main session. Not set on other tasks.

parent_task_id.description: task_id of the subagent (local_agent) task whose agent launched this subagent, shell, monitor or workflow task. Absent when the launcher is the main thread, has no task_id of its own (a teammate, an agent inside a workflow), or is no longer tracked. A resumed subagent keeps its original parent. The parent may be a foreground or already-ended task, so treat an unknown id as no parent.

ambient.description: True for tasks that are not activity (every skip_transcript task, plus every live-update watcher, requested or auto-started); hosts should exclude them from activity indicators.

awaited.description: @internal True for a run of a resumed subagent (local_agent) that the tool call which resumed it waits for, as SendMessage does when background tasks are disabled; its task_started, if one is sent, names that call in tool_use_id. The run has ended by the time that call returns or throws, even when the wait is aborted. Its report goes into that call's result, so expect no follow-up turn when it ends. A later resume that nothing waits for starts a new run without the field.

tasks.description: Every live background task after the change. REPLACE semantics: swap your set for this payload.

system_background_tasks_changedOutput.description: The full set of live background tasks, emitted whenever membership changes (start, completion, kill, a foreground agent being backgrounded) or an entry's `ambient` flag or `parent_task_id` changes. A level signal, unlike the task_started/task_notification edge bookends: consumers that only need 'is background work running' should replace their set with each payload rather than pairing edges, so a missed bookend cannot wedge a stale running indicator. Ordering relative to the bookends for the same transition is unspecified (in practice a task that starts in the background joins the level before its task_started, and a finishing task leaves it after its task_updated and task_notification), so do not correlate it with the edge stream. The level is per-process: nothing is emitted at startup, so consumers must reset to the empty set whenever the session's CLI process (re)starts and let the next membership change repopulate it. A host that re-initializes an already-running process (a repeated `initialize` control request, e.g. after reconnecting) is sent a snapshot of the current set right behind the success response to that request, even when it is empty, so it need not wait for a change; CLIs that predate this send nothing there.

seq.description: Rises by one with each of these frames this client writes (1 for the first); never reset by an init. A reader keeps the highest it has applied and drops a lower one.

changed.description: The top-level keys of `cloud_session` whose value differs from the last block this client wrote (on an init or one of these frames), e.g. ["serving"] or ["calls", "connection"]; never empty. A hint for what to redraw: the block below is complete either way.

cloud_session.description: The whole block exactly as the next init would carry it (see SDKSystemMessage.cloud_session): replace the held copy, do not merge.

system_cloud_session_deltaOutput.description: @internal Written by the headless stream-json client of a cloud-hosted session (the same client that puts `cloud_session` on its init frames), and by nothing else: the session's status changed between two inits — for instance this machine's serving word or its reason, its stream to the session (`connection`), a call it serves starting, waiting on the session's approval or ending (`calls`), a serving notice said (`notices`). Only after the first init — except from a serve-only helper (`--attach-serve`), whose stream to the session carries no init: it writes these from the start, its first (`seq` 1) listing every key of the block in `changed`, so a host that has read no init takes that frame's block as its first snapshot. At most a few per second (changes within a quarter second are written as one frame carrying the latest block); none when nothing differs. An init is always a complete snapshot, so a host that (re)attaches resynchronises from the first init it reads and applies these on top. Display-only; ignore it if you do not draw session status.

provider.description: Forge classification derived from the URL's shape: 'github', 'github-enterprise', 'gitlab', or 'bitbucket' for pull/merge requests, 'gerrit' for a change on a googlesource.com Gerrit host, and other values for other review systems in internal builds. A naming hint, not host trust — an unrecognized host with a PR-shaped path classifies as 'github-enterprise'. Open set; treat an unknown value as a valid provider you don't recognize, never as an error.

url.description: Web URL of the published change, as printed in the command output. Unverified — do not route authenticated requests to this host without your own validation.

repo.description: Repository path from the URL (owner/name on GitHub; may carry more segments on GitLab). Shape-validated (forge path segments only; exactly owner/name except on GitLab) but not verified against any forge — on GitLab a leading segment can be a nested group, so never interpret it as a host.

identifier.description: Provider-native change identifier — the PR/MR (or other change) number as a string.

action.description: What the session did that produced this announcement: the flag-aware gh pr verb it ran ('created', 'closed', 'auto-merge-enabled', …), 'pushed' for a push to a branch that has a PR (or a push that opened or updated a Gerrit change), 'checked-out' for gh pr checkout, or 'started' for the open change on the branch the session's working directory was on when a Claude Desktop session started or resumed (sent once, at the first initialize) — always sent by current producers, absent only from older ones.

branch.description: The session's working branch when it produced the change. Sent for providers whose changes have no head branch of their own ('gerrit'), so a host can place the change on that checkout, and with 'created' on any provider: the branch the create was opened from (its --head / --source-branch flag, else the working branch), so a host can show the new change before its own forge lookup answers. Absent otherwise.

system_code_change_publishedOutput.description: @internal A code change from this session went out for review (a pull/merge request, or another provider's change in internal builds). Fires when the harness sees the change published or links the session to a PR — on creation, and also when the session contributes to an existing one (gh pr edit/close/ready, gh pr checkout, a push to a branch that has an open PR) — so bind on every event, not just the first; re-emission for the same URL is possible and idempotent. Provenance: values are scraped from the command's captured output (the last PR-shaped URL printed) or a gh pr view lookup. Captured output is not only the forge CLI's own text — hook output or files printed by the same command can contribute — so treat the fields as a binding hint: display them, but verify against the forge with your own credential-scoped lookup before routing authenticated requests or trusting the host. Best-effort, not exhaustive: a crash before the link, gh printing no URL to a piped capture (gh pr merge), or an unrecognized forge means no event — keep your provider-API lookup as the source of truth and treat this as the trigger.

description.description: Description of what the skill does

aliases.description: Alternate names that resolve to this command (e.g., /cost and /stats both resolve to /usage)

builtin.description: True when the command is Claude Code's own; absent for a command defined by a user, project, plugin or MCP server. Rows can share a name: when a marked row carries it, /name runs that one, and an unmarked row is the one /name runs only when no marked row shares its name. The marker describes the row's name, not its aliases: a typed alias runs a command that has it as its name, when one exists, whatever this marker says.

plugin.description: @internal The plugin that registered the command through `$.command.register`, by name, so a client can say whose it is: the name and description are the plugin's own words. Absent for every other command, one a plugin the binary carries registered included. Untrusted text: escape it before display.

items.description: Information about an available skill (invoked via /command syntax).

system_commands_changedOutput.description: Fire-and-forget push of the full slash-command list after a mid-session change (e.g. skills discovered dynamically as the agent works in a subdirectory). Clients should REPLACE their cached command list with this payload; supportedCommands() tracks the latest push, so a re-fetch returns the same fresh list.

cumulative_dropped_tokens.description: @internal Running total of context tokens compaction has removed so far, across this and every earlier compaction. Each contribution is approximately pre_tokens − post_tokens.

user_context.description: @internal User-provided focus text for manual "summarize from here".

messages_summarized.description: @internal Count of messages the compaction summarized.

precomputed.description: @internal The summary was generated in the background at the autocompact threshold and swapped in when prompt-too-long fired; duration_ms measures user-wait from that point.

pre_compact_discovered_tools.description: @internal Deferred-tool names discovered before this compaction. extractDiscoveredToolNames reads this back on the next turn so the tool-schema filter keeps including them after the tool_reference-carrying messages were summarized away.

pre_compact_artifact_read_versions.description: @internal The artifact versions the conversation held before this compaction (slug is the artifact id, ver the version read or published), most recently changed first; empty when it held none. A resumed session replays these so it can update those artifacts without reading them again.

preserved_segment.description: Relink info for messagesToKeep. Loaders splice the preserved segment at anchor_uuid (summary for suffix-preserving, boundary for prefix-preserving partial compact) so resume includes preserved content. Unset when compaction summarizes everything (no messagesToKeep).

all_uuids.description: @internal Unfiltered messagesToKeep UUIDs. uuids is the on-disk subset (messages recordTranscript writes); all_uuids is the in-memory superset including non-loggable messages an in-process surface still holds for the next turn's API input. Absent from older producers.

preserved_messages.description: Ordered messagesToKeep UUIDs. Supersedes preserved_segment — readers look up each UUID directly and relink uuids[i] to uuids[i-1] (uuids[0] to anchor_uuid) instead of walking the parentUuid chain. Unset when compaction summarizes everything.

logical_parent_uuid.description: @internal uuid of the last pre-compact message — the backpointer forkSession follows across the compaction break. Distinct from the session-file chain parent (which is the post-compact summary). Absent from older producers.

historical.description: @internal Replayed history rather than a live message (stamped by the Remote Control bridge when it flushes history to the session server).

request_id.description: request_id of the in-flight control_request this progress belongs to.

system_control_request_progressOutput.description: Progress for a long-running client-originated control_request (currently only side_question), correlated by request_id. status 'started' means the worker accepted the request and launched the work; 'api_retry' carries the same retry counters as SDKAPIRetryMessage and is present only for that status.

kind.description: What kind of development the evidence shows. 'ios_app' from the conversation (in the main thread or a subagent): Claude ran one of Apple's tools for an iOS SDK, an iOS destination or the Simulator (xcodebuild, xcrun or swift for an iOS SDK, destination or target, simctl, devicectl), wrote iOS source into a Swift or Objective-C file (import UIKit, an import of a UIKit header, or an .iOS platform in a package manifest), or wrote or read build settings that name an iOS SDK or target iPhone or iPad; no Swift edit is needed for these. A command counts only where the shell would run it, so one that is quoted, in a here-document or in a comment does not. Weaker evidence (an iOS deployment target, any other TARGETED_DEVICE_FAMILY setting, iOS source written into another kind of file, an iOS tool named inside a quoted script) counts only beside a .swift file that Claude wrote or edited. A macOS-only app or server-side Swift package never qualifies. 'ios_app' from the project scan: the session's git repository has an Xcode project, at its root or in its ios/, iosApp/, macos/ or apple/ folder, whose build settings name an iOS SDK or target iPhone or iPad. 'android_app' from the conversation: Claude wrote or edited a .kt, .kts or .java file and something it wrote, read, or ran is Android-specific (a manifest, the Android Gradle plugin, an android.* import, adb, a Gradle variant task such as assembleDebug, the emulator), so a Kotlin server or a multiplatform module with no Android target never qualifies. 'android_app' from the project scan: the session's git repository has an AndroidManifest.xml, or the Android Gradle plugin in a build script or version catalog, at its root or in its android/ folder. More kinds will be added; ignore a kind you do not recognize.

trigger.description: The evidence the detection fired on, for a host's own analytics. From the conversation, it is the first platform-specific evidence seen, whichever order it and a file edit the rule required arrived in; an 'ios_app' detection with no Swift edit names the first evidence that is enough alone. 'ios_app': 'uikit_import' (import UIKit or .iOS( in text Claude wrote), 'xcode_project' (iOS build settings written, or seen in a tool result such as a pbxproj or xcconfig read), 'ios_command' (an iOS SDK, an iOS destination or target, or the Simulator's tools, in a command Claude ran). 'android_app': 'android_import' (import android. in text Claude wrote), 'android_manifest' (a manifest path or body written, or seen in a tool result), 'gradle_plugin' (the Android Gradle plugin written, or seen in a tool result), 'android_command' (adb, the emulator, sdkmanager, avdmanager, react-native run-android or a Gradle variant task). The edit values 'swift_edit', 'kotlin_edit' and 'java_edit' are reserved for rules that need no other evidence; no rule sends them yet. 'project_scan', for any kind: a scan of the session's git repository. The CLI scans when the process starts and sends the result. After each conversation_reset, it sends the latest scan's result again. A conversation whose scan did not find every kind scans again, uncached, when its first message arrives, so a kind that scan missed can come after that message. A client that needs to tell project evidence from conversation evidence checks for 'project_scan'. More values will be added; ignore one you do not recognize. Absent from CLI versions that predate the field, which send only conversation evidence.

system_dev_intentOutput.description: @internal The conversation, or the git repository it runs in, shows a known kind of development work, for hosts that key tooling on it (Claude Code Desktop opens its iOS Simulator entry point on ios_app). Sent with trigger as its only other payload. Per conversation per process, each kind is sent at most once from conversation evidence and at most once from the project scan. Conversation evidence is sent when it first completes, or at startup when a resumed conversation already has it. Project evidence comes from a CLI process in print mode (-p), which is how the Agent SDK and Claude Code Desktop start it. It is sent at startup, after each conversation_reset, and at the first message of a conversation whose earlier scan did not find every kind. Either can arrive before system/init. A rewind or compaction never retracts it and only a conversation_reset starts over. Treat each kind as a sticky fact about the conversation: a client that needs only the kind can ignore repeats, and one that needs to know what set it off reads trigger.

system_elicitation_completeOutput.description: Emitted when an MCP server confirms that a URL-mode elicitation is complete.

draft_id.description: UUID of the on-disk draft file under ~/.claude/feedback/drafts/ — the identity for discard and submit.

title.description: Sanitized one-line summary from the SendFeedback tool call.

details_preview.description: First ~200 chars of the sanitized details, for the host UI's three-line card preview. The full draft stays on disk and is read when the user opens the review form.

system_feedback_draft_queuedOutput.description: @internal Emitted by the SendFeedback tool after it writes a local draft to ~/.claude/feedback/drafts/, so a connected host UI can surface a review card without polling the filesystem. Carries only the card's display fields; nothing is sent anywhere without the user's explicit action on the review form.

message_uuid.description: The uuid of the inbound user message whose file_attachments named the files.

sent_count.description: How many well-formed file_attachments entries that message had.

file_uuid.description: The file_uuid of the message's file_attachments entry.

reason.description: Why, as a short code. 'download': it could not be downloaded. 'too_large': the file is over the size a session accepts, so sending it again cannot help. 'not_found': the files route answered 404 or 410: the file is most likely deleted, or is not this session's to read, so sending it again rarely helps. 'write': it was downloaded and could not be saved. 'no_token': the session had no credential to download with. 'not_finished': the step that fetches a message's files was cut short or threw, so all its files are listed, though some may have been saved. 'count_cap': the message named more files than a session fetches, and this one was over the limit. More codes may be added; read an unknown one as 'did not arrive'.

missing.description: The files Claude was told did not arrive, each once. Never empty.

system_file_attachments_missingOutput.description: @internal Some files a user message sent by reference (file_attachments) did not arrive where Claude can read them, and Claude was told so in that message's text or in a later note; the turn runs on without them. A host can use it to tell the person who sent them; a session with Remote Control on also sends it to its Remote Control clients itself. Sent once the message is queued, or later when a download or a save that runs beside its turn fails, or both; only for a message that reached the session through Claude Code Remote or over Remote Control, never for input a local host writes; whenever Claude is told, and for the same files. Queued counts as told: a message that a Stop then clears from the queue, or that a UserPromptSubmit hook then blocks, still sends it, though Claude never reads that message. Nothing is sent when every file arrives, when the message is refused or has no uuid (over Remote Control, one not in UUID form counts as none), for another session's message that was first held for approval, when the only files lost are those over the count limit of a message in which an entry carries a sha256 digest, or for a picture that reached Claude inside the message and whose saved copy alone was lost; on claude-code-server the same holds for a text file whose copy was to be written late, at a use of the tool container. A file whose entry carries a sha256 (another session's transfer) is reported to Claude by name instead, and is listed here only under 'not_finished'. Each event states the whole list for its message: a save lost after the message was queued, or a delivery to a new worker, states it again, so keep the last one per message_uuid. If its files all arrive that time nothing is sent, and the earlier event stands. One exception: a worker that takes over a turn already begun, or is sent again a message that its transcript already holds, may fetch and save the message's files again, except pictures and files with a sha256. Its event lists only those it could not fetch or save, so it can leave out a picture an earlier event listed, and can list a file the earlier worker did save.

level.description: Render level. 'info' shows only in transcript mode; 'notice' renders in inactive gray; 'suggestion' and 'warning' are more prominent.

tool_use_id.description: Dedupes progress messages for the same tool use.

prevent_continuation.description: When true, execution stops after this message (e.g. a Stop hook denied continuation).

tag.description: Opaque feature tag on a line a host may treat specially; absent on ordinary lines. Hosts ignore values they do not know.

no_verdict_kind.description: Sent with kind 'no_verdict', and says why: 'remote_run_failed' (the hook runs on another machine, and the run failed or gave no usable answer), 'remote_run_timed_out' (the wait for that run timed out; the hook may never have been sent), 'interrupted' (the turn was aborted during that wait), 'remote_runner_refused' (Claude Code does not send this hook to that machine; a retry does not help), 'unsupported_in_cloud_session' (a cloud session cannot run this type of hook), 'output_distrusted' (Claude Code could not prove that it read all of the hook's output), 'callback_timed_out' (a callback hook did not answer in time), 'hook_failed' and 'hook_timed_out' (for this hook a failure blocks), 'hooks_never_ran' (an internal fault: the hooks did not run over the submitted text), 'personal_config_refused' (the session restricts personal config, and part of the person's own settings did not load or is off), 'rewrite_unplaceable' (a plugin's code module changed the prompt's text, and Claude Code has no place to put the change).

prompt_submit_outcome.description: @internal Present on the line that ends a submitted prompt before a model call. It says how the prompt ended, so a host can write its own message or count endings and does not match `content`. kind: 'blocked_by_hook' (a hook answered with a block), 'stopped_by_hook' (a hook answered continue:false), 'dropped_by_hook' (a plugin's code module dropped the prompt), 'not_passed_on' (a plugin's code module answered and did not pass the prompt on), 'no_verdict' (no hook gave a verdict, and Claude Code ended the prompt itself). prompt_kept: true when the prompt stays in the conversation, where the model reads it on the next turn. Do not infer it from kind. reason: the hook's text as Claude Code got it, with nothing added here; a model writes it for a prompt or agent hook. It is never sent with no_verdict. It is absent when Claude Code got no text, and for a plugin's code module that blocks on the UserPromptSubmit hook event. ANSI codes are removed, control and invisible characters are replaced, line feeds stay, and long text is cut. It is untrusted and can quote the prompt, so render it as plain text. A cloud session can run the hook on another machine: its tool container, where any program can write reason, or the person's own machine. reason is then what that machine sent, for a block and for a stop. The person's own machine puts a label before the stderr of an exit 2, or before 'No stderr output' when there is none. Either machine makes the block itself when it could not read all of the hook's output, and the person's own machine can do so when its timeout fires. Each reads 'blocked_by_hook', with that machine's sentence as reason. Claude Code's own block for an SDK host that reconnected before its hook answered reads the same way, with Claude Code's sentence as reason. New values can appear: treat an unknown value as absent, and ignore reason beside an unknown kind. A slash command that runs as a fork does not send this key when a hook ends it. A follow-up that a hook blocks while a turn runs carries this key too, so read it as the end of a turn only when the next result has num_turns 0.

system_informationalOutput.description: Generic text banner emitted by the loop — non-error status lines, hook feedback (e.g. a UserPromptSubmit hook's block reason), slash-command output. Hosts render `content` as plaintext at the given level.

kept_request_ids.description: The request ids of the earlier worker's asks that this worker keeps answerable.

system_inherited_asks_settledOutput.description: @internal A cloud worker's report, before its first turn, of which asks it inherited and keeps. Any ask stored before this event that it does not name is over.

apiKeySource.description: Where the credential used for API requests came from: 'ANTHROPIC_API_KEY' (environment variable), 'apiKeyHelper' (the configured helper command), '/login managed key' (an API key created and stored by /login with an Anthropic Console account), or 'none' (no API key in use - e.g. claude.ai OAuth login, a bearer token, or a third-party cloud provider). 'user' | 'project' | 'org' | 'temporary' | 'oauth' are legacy members that current CLIs never emit; they remain only so the type stays backward compatible.

startup_timing.description: @internal Cold-start telemetry for hosted (CCR) sessions: named startup phases and resume-hydration counters (StartupTiming in src/utils/startupTiming.ts). Absent elsewhere.

source.description: Where the server definition came from — same values as McpServerStatus.source (sdk | plugin | a config scope). Absent on CLIs that predate the field.

permissionMode.description: Permission mode for controlling how tool executions are handled. 'default' - Standard behavior, prompts for dangerous operations. 'acceptEdits' - Auto-accept file edit operations. 'bypassPermissions' - Bypass all permission checks (requires allowDangerouslySkipPermissions). 'plan' - Planning mode, no actual tool execution. 'dontAsk' - Don't prompt for permissions, deny if not pre-approved. 'auto' - Use a model classifier to approve/deny permission prompts.

terminal_slash_commands.description: Subset of slash_commands whose UX is bound to the local terminal (e.g. exit, statusline). Phone/remote UIs should hide these from command menus; desktop surfaces may keep them. Present only when non-empty; absent on CLIs that predate the field, and on sessions where no advertised command carries the tag.

source.description: @internal Plugin source identifier in "name\@marketplace" format. Sentinels: "name\@inline" for --plugin-dir, "name\@skills-dir" for .claude/skills plugins, "name\@synced" for plugins synced from claude.ai, "name\@builtin" for built-in plugins.

version.description: The plugin's version as declared in its plugin.json manifest, emitted verbatim (plugin-author-controlled — validate before trusting). Omitted when the manifest declares no version.

path.description: Present only when a --plugin-dir, SDK `plugins` or synced directory entry did not load at all: the path of that entry, resolved against the cwd (for a directory, the value its `plugins[]` row would have carried; for a .zip, the archive; a --plugin-url entry carries none). `plugin` is then the positional `inline[N]` / `synced[N]` tag, so a host that mounts several directories pairs the error to its own by this path.

plugin_errors.description: Plugin load-time errors. A plugin that did not load (an unmet dependency, a --plugin-dir entry that failed) is absent from `plugins[]`; a plugin that loaded without one of its components keeps its row and gets an entry here too. `plugin` is `name@marketplace`, or the positional `inline[N]` / `synced[N]` tag for a directory entry that failed before it had a name; `type` is a category from an open set (path-not-found, generic-error, manifest-validation-error, dependency-unsatisfied, hook-load-failed, …) — treat a value you do not recognize as a generic failure; `message` is display text. The key is omitted when there are no errors; CI can fail on `(plugin_errors?.length ?? 0) > 0`. A session whose frames are persisted server-side (a Remote Control worker) always omits this key — plugin diagnostics stay in the local log there, so an omitted key does not assert a clean load.

plugin_warnings.description: @internal Plugin authoring feedback (e.g., a default folder shadowed by a manifest key). When `plugin` matches an entry in `plugins[]`, that plugin loaded and the warning is advisory; warnings with a synthetic `plugin` source (no matching `plugins[]` entry, e.g. workspace-level suppression notices) describe content that did NOT load. The key is omitted when there are no warnings. On connections that persist frames server-side (the local bridge-worker lane) this key is always omitted — plugin diagnostics stay in the local log, so an omitted key there does NOT assert a clean load.

mcp_server_errors.description: @internal MCP server config entries from --mcp-config that failed validation and were skipped (e.g. a `url` entry with no `type`). Affected servers are absent from `mcp_servers[]`. `type` is a stable category from an open set — currently unknown_type, url_missing_type, invalid_config, reserved_name, or (Remote Control child only) bridge_carrier_foreign_entry, bridge_carrier_not_http, bridge_carrier_url_mismatch, bridge_carrier_no_ingress_origin, bridge_carrier_no_session_id; treat values you do not recognize as a generic skip. The key is omitted when there are no errors; CI can fail on `(mcp_server_errors?.length ?? 0) > 0`.
